_comment: Construction materials added from ecoinvent by `ecoinvent_add_materials`.
One 'market for' dataset per product (it includes transport to the market),
Rest-of-World where ecoinvent has one, else Global: there are no Mexican
datasets in 3.12-sandbox. Picked from a search on 2026-10-26; the second
batch (mortars, plasters, gypsum, aggregates, bricks, scrap steels) on 2026-11-06.
The category becomes the name's prefix, which is how the explorer groups
materials. Units are ecoinvent's reference units, so refreshes never skip
'description' is ecoinvent's own text from the product's production
dataset ('description_from'), with ecoinvent's standard notices removed:
a market dataset only carries a generic paragraph about markets.

Background:
This activity represents the production of primary low-alloyed steel in a basic oxygen furnace (BOF), a discontinuous process involving the following steps: 1) pretreatment of hot metal (pig iron) from the blast furnace (desulphurisation, deslagging, etc.); 2) mixing of charge (including alloying additions), weighing, transfer and reladling ; 3) oxidation in the BOF (decarburisation and oxidation of impurities); 4) secondary metallurgical treatment in a ladle furnace; and 5) casting (continuous and/or ingot).

Modelling approach:
Data on were mostly taken from the IPPC Best Available Technology report from the European Commission (Remus et al., 2013); note that where only data ranges were provided, the geometric mean of reported values was used here. The proportion of each by-product that is recycled internally (i.e. returned as an input to the process after it has been produced) is based on measured data from plants worldwide reported by worldsteel (2010): slag (including desulphurisation slag, BOF slag, slag from secondary metallurgy and slag from continuous casting), 14%; spittings, 100%; dust and sludge, 22%; and mill scale, 89%.

References:
Remus, R., Aguado-Monsonet, M. A., Roudier, S. & Samcho, L. D. (2013). JRC reference report - Best available techniques (BAT) reference document for iron and steel production. Joint Research Centre - European Commission, Luxemboug.
Worldsteel (2010). Steel industry by-products. World Steel Association: Brussels, Belgium.

Background:
This activity represents the production of primary steel (carbon; unalloyed) in a basic oxygen furnace (BOF), a discontinuous process involving the following steps: 1) pretreatment of hot metal (pig iron) from the blast furnace (desulphurisation, deslagging, etc.); 2) mixing of charge, weighing, transfer and reladling ; 3) oxidation in the BOF (decarburisation and oxidation of impurities); 4) secondary metallurgical treatment in a ladle furnace; and 5) casting (continuous and/or ingot).

Modelling approach:
Data on were mostly taken from the IPPC Best Available Technology report from the European Commission (Remus et al., 2013); note that where only data ranges were provided, the geometric mean of reported values was used here. The proportion of each by-product that is recycled internally (i.e. returned as an input to the process after it has been produced) is based on measured data from plants worldwide reported by worldsteel (2010): slag (including desulphurisation slag, BOF slag, slag from secondary metallurgy and slag from continuous casting), 14%; spittings, 100%; dust and sludge, 22%; and mill scale, 89%.

The ratio of pig iron to iron scrap inputs was based on average data from European steelmakers. The values were then adjusted to ensure Fe balance. This ratio is, however, highly variable among regions, globally, and the value used may not be representative of a) the average global situation or b) the situation in other regions. We advise caution when appliying these data elsewhere.
References:
Remus, R., Aguado-Monsonet, M. A., Roudier, S. & Samcho, L. D. (2013). JRC reference report - Best available techniques (BAT) reference document for iron and steel production. Joint Research Centre - European Commission, Luxemboug.

Background:
This activity represents the production of stainless steel (Type 304, aka. 18/8; assumed composition 68.6% Fe, 9.3% Ni, 19.0% Cr and 0.08% C) in a two-stage process. Raw materials (charge chrome, carbon steel scrap and ferronickel) are loaded into an electric arc furnace (EAF) and melted together. The composition of the charge corresponds to that of the desired steel product, besides the carbon content. The molten metal is then removed from the EAF and transferred to an argon-oxygen decarburisation (AOD) refining vessel, in which the amounts of impurities, principally carbon, are reduced to the desired levels. The purified molten metal is then continuously cast into stainless steel slabs (Norgate et al., 2004).

Modelling approach:
Data on the use of electricity, oxygen, argon and electrodes were taken from Norgate et al. (2004) and are specific to stainless steel production. The amounts of steel by-products (dusts, sludges and slags) that are produced are based on measured data from plants worldwide reported by worldsteel (2010). Also based on worldsteel (2010), the following internal recycling rates (i.e. returned as an input to the process after it has been produced) were assumed: EAF slag, 3%; secondary metallurgy slag, 14%; and dust, 10%. All other data were taken from the IPPC Best Available Technology report from the European Commission (Remus et al., 2013) and are representative of typical low- and un-alloyed steel production in an electric arc furnace in Europe. Note that where only data ranges were provided, the geometric mean of reported values was used here.

References:
Norgate, Jahanshahi, S. & Rankin, W. J. (2004). Alternative routes to stainless steel - a life cycle approach. Proceedings: Tenth International Ferroalloys Congress; INFACON X: ‘Transformation through Technology’, 1 – 4 February 2004, Cape Town, South Africa.
Remus, R., Aguado-Monsonet, M. A., Roudier, S. & Samcho, L. D. (2013). JRC reference report - Best available techniques (BAT) reference document for iron and steel production. Joint Research Centre - European Commission, Luxemboug.
Worldsteel (2010). Steel industry by-products. World Steel Association: Brussels, Belgium.

materials.description:
This dataset describes the production of concrete blocks in the Global geography.
The dataset includes the reception of materials, dosing and mixing, block production by vibration, curing and storage.

Current production technology. The dataset covers the main technologies for concrete block production in Brazil and Ecuador. The manufacturing process begins by dosing and mixing the cement, aggregates and water to make concrete. In the block machine, the steel cast is filled with concrete and the block is shaped and compacted by vibration. The fresh concrete block is then transported to the curing chambers. The cure can be done in the following ways: 1) naturally, leaving the blocks in closed chambers with no water addition; 2) wet cure, spraying water over the blocks to keep relative humidity high in order to ensure proper hydration of the cement; 3) thermal cure with steam, which enables the cement to hydrate faster than in the wet cure and lowers concrete shrinkage. The blocks are then packed in pallets and stored. The process can happen with various automation levels and different types and sizes of block machines. It is common to produce various block shapes and compressive strength classes in a single factory, as well as concrete pavers.

materials.description:
Hardening is assumed to be by air-drying. It is assumed that there is wastewater and solid waste, but as no exact description on the composition of the wastewater and solid waste is available a proxy for each ("treatment, concrete production effluent, to wastewater treatment, class 3" and "disposal, municipal solid waste, 22.9% water, to municipal incineration") is used. The lifespan of the plant is assumed to be 50 years.
Autoclaved Aerated Concrete is a Lightweight, Load-bearing, High-insulating, Durable building product, which is produced in a wide range of sizes and strengths. AAC Blocks is lightweight and compare to the red bricks AAC blocks are three times lighter.
The Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (AAC) material was developed in 1924 in Sweden. It has become one of the most used building materials in Europe and is rapidly growing in many other countries around the world.
AAC is produced from the common materials lime, sand, cement and water, and a small amount of rising agent. After mixing and molding, it is then autoclaved under heat and pressure to create its unique properties. AAC has excellent thermal insulation and acoustic absorption properties. AAC is fire and pest resistant, and is economically and environmentally superior to the more traditional structural building materials such as concrete, wood, brick and stone.
AAC is a highly thermally insulating concrete-based material used for both internal and external construction. Besides AAC's insulating capability, one of its advantages in construction is its quick and easy installation, because the material can be routed, sanded, or cut to size on site using standard carbon steel power tools.
AAC is well suited for urban areas with high rise buildings and those with high temperature variations. Due to its lower density, high rise buildings constructed using AAC require less steel and concrete for structural members. The requirement of mortar for laying of AAC blocks is reduced due to the lower number of joints. Similarly, the material required for rendering is also lower due to the dimensional accuracy of AAC. The increased thermal efficiency of AAC makes it suitable for use in areas with extreme temperatures, as it eliminates the need for separate materials for construction and insulation, leading to faster construction and cost savings.

This dataset was created as a weighted average (by production volumes) of the regional clinker production activities.
The dataset describes the production of portland cement clinker; in the production different types of alternative fuels and raw materials are used.
Clinker is the active component of Portland cement that, once mixed with water, contributes to the hardening of the cement itself. As a result, clinker plays a fundamental role in the production of various construction materials, including cements, concretes, and mortars. The manufacturing of clinker is highly energy-intensive and requires a significant amount of raw materials.
Large amounts of limestone, along with additional raw materials like sand, clay, iron ore, and other corrective materials—roughly 1.7 tons of these materials per ton of clinker—are thermochemically processed in order to produce clinker. Kiln ovens, as well as associated infrastructure and equipment, are needed for this process. The kiln oven must maintain high temperatures because alite, a crucial mineral in the composition of clinker that gives concrete most of its initial strength after hydration, must form at a temperature of roughly 1450°C. In order to maintain these high temperatures, a significant amount of secondary fuels (wastes) as well as conventional fuels are used to produce this energy.
The kiln technology and fuel mix are highly dependent on geographical factors.

Clinker manufacturing begins with the collection and transportation of raw materials to the production site. The raw materials are crushed, mixed, and milled into a raw meal, which is then processed in a kiln oven. Depending on available technologies, the kiln can be either a wet or a long dry type, with the latter requiring lower energy input. Current technologies may include preheaters and precalciners, further reducing energy requirements before the raw meal enters the dry kiln.
The principal chemical reactions during pyroprocessing for clinker production are:
CaCO3 => CaO + CO2 (800°C–900°C)
2CaO + SiO2 => (CaO)2⋅SiO2 (800°C–900°C)
3CaO + Al2O3 => (CaO)3⋅Al2O3 (900°C–1300°C)
4CaO + Al2O3 + Fe2O3 => (CaO)4⋅Al2O3⋅Fe2O3 (900°C–1300°C)
CaO + (CaO)2.SiO2 => (CaO)3⋅SiO2 (>1300°C)
Following pyroprocessing in the kiln, rapid cooling is necessary to preserve the high-temperature phase assemblage, which is thermodynamically unstable at intermediate temperatures but metastably preserved at lower temperatures due to energy and mixing barriers.

This dataset represents the mixing of cement mortar in the GLO geography. The raw materials are mixed in a ratio defined by best construction practices and literature values. Subsequently, the mixture is transported and packaged. Mix ratios can vary. For example, 1 part cement to 2.5 parts sand is used for a rich mix suitable for structural brickwork such as manholes in roads. A mix of 1 part cement to 7 parts sand is suitable for applications requiring greater flexibility or movement. No direct process emissions are taken into account as they play a subordinate role compared to the emissions of the raw material production (e.g. drying of silica sand). For the infrastructure inventory, a yearly production amount of 150'000 tons of an Austrian producer is assumed. The lifespan of the machines is assumed to be 20 years.

Relevant literature:
Zhang, H. (2011): Building Mortar. Chapter 6 in "Building Materials in Civil Engineering", Woodhead publishing series in Civil and Structural Engineering, Pages 150-169, 423. https://doi.org/10.1533/9781845699567.150.
Claisse, P. A. (2016): Mortars and grouts. Civil Engineering Materials, 303–311. doi:10.1016/b978-0-08-100275-9.00028-0.“

'Mortar' refers to a mixture of a binding agent with fine aggregates. Mortars are mixed with water prior to their application. Cement mortar is a mortar that uses cement as the binding agent, together with fine aggregates such as sand. The main difference between cement mortar and concrete is that there is no coarse aggregate in mortar. Therefore, 'cement mortar' can also be called 'fine aggregate concrete'. Cement mortar is typically produced through a mechanical mixing process, in which the raw materials required by the specified mix design are combined. This mixing process ensures uniform distribution of cement, aggregates and the possible use of admixtures (not included in this dataset) to achieve the desired consistency and properties. Once mixed, the cement mortar is transported via conveyor belts, bagged and stored, ready for delivery to the construction site.
Cement mortar is mostly used in structural engineering applications, including the binding of stones, bricks, blocks and for filling the gaps in walls. The manufacturing of cement mortar in this dataset is assumed to follow the current technology level.

Plastering is done on the walls to remove surface imperfections, maintain line level and alignment. In addition to that it also acts as a protective surface for external walls. Cement plaster, Gypsum plaster and Lime plaster are the commonly used plastering materials for house constructions. Cement plaster is made by mixing cement and sand in the proportions required. Cement plaster is applied to both interior and exterior walls to give them a smooth surface.
The differences between mortar and plaster lie in the capacity of plasters to take better finish, which depend to a very large extent on the type of sand used in the mix. For plasters we use finer sand. However in mortar we use coarse particles of sand.
Mix ratio is the volumetric mixing ratio of cement and aggregates. Mix Ratio varies from 1:3 to 1:6 depending upon the application area. The mix ratio accounted for this dataset is 1:6. This dataset considered hand-mixed on site production and its application is for plastering larger area like big buildings.

Mixing of cement, water and aggregates done by hand mixing.

materials.description:
This dataset has been extrapolated from the corresponding IN dataset. A concrete slab is a common structural element of modern buildings. Horizontal slabs of steel reinforced concrete, typically between 4 and 20 inches (100 and 500 millimeters) thick, are most often used to construct floors and ceilings, while thinner slabs are also used for exterior paving.

In many domestic and industrial buildings a thick concrete slab, supported on foundations or directly on the subsoil, is used to construct the ground floor of a building. These can either be "ground-bearing" or "suspended" slabs. For Double-storey or Multi-storey buildings, the use of a few common types of concrete suspended slabs are used. In high rise buildings and skyscrapers, thinner, pre-cast concrete slabs are slung between the steel frames to form the floors and ceilings on each level. Cast in-Situ slabs which used in high rise buildings and huge shopping complexes as well as houses. These in-situ slabs are cast on site using shutters and reinforced steel.

On the technical drawings, reinforced concrete slabs are often abbreviated to "r.c.c.slab" or simply "r.c." Technical drawings are often created by structural Engineers who use software such as AutoCad or Revit structure

Two types of concrete used to cast slab: Ready mixed concrete and Hand/Machine mix concrete. Hand mix concrete are rearly used in slab casting.

Current production technology. This dataset is a copy of the EC geography, and considered representative of the global production of adobe bricks. The manufacturing process includes the reception of raw materials, dosing, mixing, forming, drying, and storage of adobe bricks. The overall process applied in Ecuador implies that a selection of 2 or 3 types of clay is prepared, and mixed with straw and rainwater. The mix is made with the help of the trampling of a horse, then placed in a wooden mold with the shape of a brick (forming process, done by hands). The material in excess on the surface is taken away and reused for the next brick. The mass in the mold is left to dry under the sun. No electricity powered machine nor heat are used during the whole process.

Thi dataset is extrapolated from the IN corresponding dataset. Pulverized fuel ash-lime bricks are obtained from materials consisting of pulverized fuel ash in major quantity, lime and an accelerator acting as a catalyst. Pulverized fuel ash-lime bricks are generally manufactured by intergrading blending various raw materials are then moulded into bricks and subjected to curing cycles at different temperatures and pressures. These bricks are suitable for use in masonry construction just like common burnt clay bricks.

Fly ash, Lime, Gypsum and Sand are manually feed into a pan mixer where water is added to the required proportion for homogeneous mixing. The proportion of raw material may vary depending upon quality of raw materials. After mixing, the mixture are allowed to belt conveyor through feed in to automatic brick making machine were the bricks are pressed automatically. Then the bricks are placed on wooden pallets and kept as it is for two days thereafter transported to open area where they are water cured for 10 -15 days. The bricks are sorted and tested before dispatch.

This dataset describes mining of natural sand from riverbed deposits and its processing. Pumps dredge the slurry, which consists of sand, water, clay, silt, and gravel, from the river bed. The sand is separated from the slurry and transported by a vessel to the loading ports, where the sand is washed to clean fines and transported to the storage piles and loaded in trucks for delivery (does not the delivery itself). The sand’s coproducts (clay, silt, and gravel) return to the river during the process not being recovered for economic purposes, furthermore they don’t receive any allocation. Sand is not sorted by grain size in this dataset.
The dataset includes the sand extraction and processing,  as well as equipment maintenance. Machinery is taken into account within the dataset "diesel, burned in building machine", as all machinery runs on diesel. Administration buildings and the quarry’s end of life are not taken into account. Data were collected from literature and some additional data were measured in one quarry located in the state of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, with current technology.
The representativeness of the dataset on a national scale is low ( >1%).

Typical technology for sand dredging in Brazil.
The technology involves two steps: extraction and processing. Sand is the only product from this process, even though gravel can be extracted, it is not recovered. Suction Hopper Dredger (autonomous vessels that perform all stages of sand mining, i.e., extraction, loading, transport, and unloading) is considered. Extraction and loading stages are executed by centrifugal pumps powered by diesel engines. The pumps dredge the sand from the riverbed, along with water, clay, silt, and gravel, are extracted, forming the slurry. This fluid is pumped through the pipeline up to the vessel top where it is poured into steel sieves. Coarse materials (gravel, leaves, and sticks) are retained by the sieves and are returned to the river. The rest of the slurry (sand, water, and mud) falls into big chambers inside the vessel. Sand decants faster from the slurry, due its density and size, and deposits at the chamber’s bottom. Most of the water overflows from the vessel to the river, carrying a great amount of the mud (silt and clay). Auxiliary suction pumps drain water surplus of the sand to lower the cargo weight.
After completing the extraction and loading stages, the same vessel transports the dredged sand until loading ports. The pulp is then pumped to the loading port by pipelines to semi-closed chambers at the loading port. Sand deposits at the bottom of the port’s chambers, water returns to the river carrying part of the fines. Some companies may sort the sand by grain size in this stage. In the end, Sand is washed to clean the fines and is transported by heavy equipment to storage piles.
Dredged sand from alluvial deposits can generate several local environmental issues. Problems related with changes in the natural sedimentation process, erosion of margins, changes in the stream bed conditions, changes in the suspended sediments of river water and even problems related with local and regional sand availability. “Continued and indiscriminate sand mining not only changes the physical characteristics of the river basin environments, but also disturbs its closely linked flora, fauna, and human life” (PADMALAL; MAYA, 2014)
None of these problems were assessed in this dataset due the lack of data, but they should be taken in consideration.
For further information, please refer to Padmalal, D. & Maya, K., 2014. Sand Mining, Dordrecht: Springer Netherlands. Available at: http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-94-017-9144-1.

The activity represents the production of 1 kg of steel, structural, 100% scrap in an Electric Arc Furnace (EAF), considering a metal feedstock (excluding alloying elements) composed of 100% ferrous scrap. The alloying elements added to meet the target composition are considered to be supplied by primary production. The steel modelled in this dataset follows the following standard:
EN 10025 S355,
ASTM A572Gr50.
The composition of the modelled steel is: Fe: 98.01%, C: 0.23%, Si: 0.05%, Mn: 1.6%, P: 0.06%, S: 0.05%, %, V: Not Specified, Nb: Not Specified, Ti: Not Specified, Al: Not Specified, Cr: Not Specified, Ni: Not Specified, W: Not Specified, Cu: Not Specified, Mo: Not Specified.
The modelled steel has a yield strength of 355 MPa, a tensile strength of 470-630 MPa and a Young Modulus of 205GPa.The process comprises the following operations:
-	mixing and pretreatment (if required) of ferrous materials (including alloying additions), principally ferrous scrap;
-	furnace charging and scrap melting;
-	steel and scrap tapping;
-	secondary metallurgical treatment in a ladle furnace;
-	casting: the dataset is valid both for ingot or continuous casting, with the latter being the dominant product.
Structural steel is a category of steel specifically manufactured for use in construction and infrastructure projects where the material must bear significant loads and stresses. The steel is typically used for:
- construction: in buildings, structural steel is the backbone of many modern structures, from skyscrapers and stadiums to warehouses and residential homes. It is used for beams, columns, and frameworks that support the entire structure.  Another use in construction is for bridges: Steel is ideal for bridge construction due to its high strength-to-weight ratio and ability to withstand heavy loads and dynamic forces.
- Industrial: in the mining industry steel is used for underground and surface mining equipment, as well as for the construction of mine shafts and support structures. For factories and warehouse, steel is used for the framework of industrial buildings, providing large open spaces and the ability to support heavy machinery and equipment.
- Transportation: in railways is steel is used for train tracks, railway bridges, and rolling stock.  It is possible to build also bigger products like ships, Steel is the primary material used in shipbuilding due to its strength, weldability, and resistance to corrosion.  Modelling approach:
The alloy is built using as a base data taken from the IPPC Best Available Technology report from the European Commission (Remus et al., 2013); note that where only data ranges were provided, the geometric mean of reported values was used here. The proportion of each by-product that is recycled internally (i.e. returned as an input to the process after it has been produced) is based on measured data from plants worldwide reported by worldsteel (2010): EAF slag, 3%; secondary metallurgy slag, 14%; and dust, 10%. The recycling is not displayed in the dataset because, since it is internal, it never leaves the system boundaries.
The data taken from the IPCC BAT report were then expanded to build a model that calculates the amount of alloying element needed to satisfy the final alloy composition. To perform these calculations, the yield of the scrap was taken, together with the yield of the alloying elements. All the values used as yield for the oxidation processes are taken from literature value (specific literature reported in each exchange).
References:
Remus, R., Aguado-Monsonet, M. A., Roudier, S. & Samcho, L. D. (2013). JRC reference report - Best available techniques (BAT) reference document for iron and steel production. Joint Research Centre - European Commission, Luxemboug.
Worldsteel (2010). Steel industry by-products. World Steel Association: Brussels, Belgium.

materials.description:
The activity represents the production of 1 kg of steel, bearing, 100% scrap in an Electric Arc Furnace (EAF), considering a metal feedstock (excluding alloying elements) composed of 100% ferrous scrap. The alloying elements added to meet the target composition are considered to be supplied by primary production. The steel modelled in this dataset follows the following standard:
ASTM A295 52100
EN ISO 683-17:2023 100Cr6
The composition of the modelled steel is: Fe: 98.31%, C: 1.05%, Si: 0.25%, Mn: 0.35%, P: 0.025%, S: 0.015%, %, V: Not Specified, Nb: Not Specified, Ti: Not Specified, Al: Not Specified, Cr: 1.5%, Ni: 0.25%, W: Not Specified, Cu: Not Specified, Mo: Not Specified.
The modelled steel has a yield strength of 500 MPa, a tensile strength of 550-700 MPa and a Young Modulus of 205GPa.The process comprises the following operations:
-	mixing and pretreatment (if required) of ferrous materials (including alloying additions), principally ferrous scrap;
-	furnace charging and scrap melting;
-	steel and scrap tapping;
-	secondary metallurgical treatment in a ladle furnace;
-	casting: the dataset is valid both for ingot or continuous casting, with the latter being the dominant product.
Bearing steel refers to a class of high-carbon chromium alloy steels specifically designed for manufacturing ball, roller, and other types of bearings. These steels are engineered to withstand high cyclic contact stresses, rolling contact fatigue, and wear while maintaining dimensional stability.This type of steel is typically used for:
-	bearing components: Its high fatigue strength and resistance to rolling contact make it ideal for ball bearings, roller bearings, and other bearing components, especially in demanding applications like aerospace and automotive industries.
-	High-stress components: Due to its high tensile strength, bearing steel is used in components subjected to significant loads, such as gears, shafts, and machine parts operating under high stress.
-	Precision tools and dies: Its ability to hold a sharp edge and resist wear makes it suitable for cutting tools, punches, and dies used in manufacturing processes.
Overall, bearing steel steel is a versatile material that finds applications in various industries where reliability, durability, and precision are critical factors.Modelling approach:
The alloy is built using as a base data taken from the IPPC Best Available Technology report from the European Commission (Remus et al., 2013); note that where only data ranges were provided, the geometric mean of reported values was used here. The proportion of each by-product that is recycled internally (i.e. returned as an input to the process after it has been produced) is based on measured data from plants worldwide reported by worldsteel (2010): EAF slag, 3%; secondary metallurgy slag, 14%; and dust, 10%. The recycling is not displayed in the dataset because, since it is internal, it never leaves the system boundaries.
The data taken from the IPCC BAT report were then expanded to build a model that calculates the amount of alloying element needed to satisfy the final alloy composition. To perform these calculations, the yield of the scrap was taken, together with the yield of the alloying elements. All the values used as yield for the oxidation processes are taken from literature value (specific literature reported in each exchange).
References:
Remus, R., Aguado-Monsonet, M. A., Roudier, S. & Samcho, L. D. (2013). JRC reference report - Best available techniques (BAT) reference document for iron and steel production. Joint Research Centre - European Commission, Luxemboug.
Worldsteel (2010). Steel industry by-products. World Steel Association: Brussels, Belgium.
